title: Minimize service surge during GPU pool upgrades
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Problem: Upgrades to Dedicated GPU pools (LTS channel rollouts and node-level runtime upgrades) cause short-lived traffic surges and transient tail latency spikes when many nodes drain simultaneously or when autoscaler reacts late. We have observed two root contributors: 1) uncoordinated drain windows that overlap with autoscaler bursts, and 2) lack of pre-reserved buffer capacity for staged canary waves across LTS channels. This ticket defines a capacity-safe rollout mechanism to minimize user-visible surge during pool upgrades.

Goals:
- Ensure 99.9% of requests meet existing latency SLOs during rolling upgrades.
- Limit request shedding to controlled canary fractions rather than system-wide spikes.
- Support multi-LTS-channel pinning: upgrades to newer LTS should respect pinned nodes and per-customer capacity reservations.
- Provide deterministic rollback points and fast fallback to older model variants when capacity is constrained.

Design proposal (high level):
1) Upgrade Phases and Wave Planning: orchestrator produces a wave plan per pool that includes a pre-flight capacity reservation (ReserveBudget), a soft-drain window, and a ramped canary fraction. Waves are sized using recent RPS/token-rate percentiles to calculate the required warm standby capacity.
2) Autoscaler Handshake v2: implement a 3-step handshake between the orchestrator and cluster autoscaler: RequestReserve(capacityEstimate) -> AutoscalerAck(reservedNodes) -> StartDrain(waveId, drainBudget). AutoscalerAck includes node identifiers and an eviction budget. If Autoscaler cannot reserve, orchestrator pauses and evaluates fallback policies.
3) Soft-evict algorithm: instead of immediate hard eviction, mark nodes as DRAINING_SOFT. New requests are routed with a weighted preference away from draining nodes; long-lived KV cache contexts are migrated gradually via prefix-aware handoff. This reduces sudden cache misses.
4) Prefix/KV-aware drain windows: for pools serving long chat sessions we apply token-aware drain windows where clients with active KV sessions get extended TTLs and are moved to pinned nodes until session end, avoiding mass KV cache invalidation.
5) Canary gating and roll thresholds: implement a gate evaluation engine that uses short-window error and latency metrics, token-cost and capacity headroom. Gates include: latency_gate (p50/p95/p99 thresholds), error_rate_gate, queue_depth_gate, and cost_headroom_gate. Canary ramps are exponential but bounded (e.g., 1%, 5%, 20%). If any gate trips, orchestrator pauses and attempts a remediation step (increase reserve, slow ramp, or roll back).
6) Warm Standby Pools & Cross-Channel Borrowing: maintain a small pool of warm standby nodes per-region that can be borrowed during upgrades. For customers with pinned LTS lanes, implement soft borrowing with strict billing/notification rules.
7) Observability and SLO contracts: new rollout dashboards that show per-wave metrics (reserved vs used capacity, drain completion ETA, gate evaluations, per-customer impacted requests). We will emit structured events for audit/telemetry for each handshake step and gate decision.

Runbook and rollback: document step-by-step runbook: how to pause orchestrator, how to force immediate fallback to previous model variant, and how to expand ReserveBudget. Add an automated emergency rollback that can be triggered when p99 latency > baseline + 40% for 3 minutes.

Backward compatibility and LTS handling: when upgrading an LTS channel, the orchestrator must respect pinned-node annotations and compute required reserve only from non-pinned capacity. New release artifacts must be tagged with lts-channel metadata and rollout waves scoped accordingly.

Implementation tasks (sprint-level):
- Orchestrator: wave planner, handshake state machine, gate evaluation engine.
- Autoscaler: ability to atomically reserve nodes and report eviction budgets, API extension for AutoscalerAck.
- Runtime: DRAINING_SOFT node state and prefix-aware KV migration hooks.
- Router: weighted request routing that respects node drain weights and canary fractions.
- Console: rollout dashboard, per-wave metrics, gate decision traces.
- Runbook: emergency rollback automation and playbook.

Success metrics:
- No more than 5% increase in p99 during upgrades across test clusters compared to baseline.
- Reduction of incident pages triggered by upgrades by 90%.
- Canary gate false positives under 2% (i.e., gates do not block benign waves more than 2% of the time).

Why this is different from previous work: prior tickets focused on phased drains and evacuation scheduling. This ticket centralizes the autoscaler handshake, adds a ReserveBudget concept, introduces soft-evict/prefix-aware migration, and formalizes gates and warm-standby borrowing for LTS-sensitive upgrades.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How large must Warm Standby be to be cost-effective across regions? (ops/finance tradeoff).
- How to account for cross-tenant borrowing and billing for temporarily borrowed capacity?
- Risk of stateful session migration complexity vs simplicity of forcing session TTLs to expire.

Next steps: prototype the AutoscalerAck API and orchestrator wave planner in a staging pool; run a chaos experiment with intentional node drains and measure p99 and KV cache miss amplification.
acceptance_criteria: Orchestrator implements ReserveBudget and produces wave plans in staging
Autoscaler can acknowledge reserve requests and return eviction budgets in staging
Router honors DRAINING_SOFT weights and moves new requests away from draining nodes
Canary gate evaluation engine triggers pause/rollback when thresholds are breached in simulated tests
Console shows per-wave metrics and gate decisions for at least two staging rollouts
Runbook includes an automated rollback trigger based on p99 latency threshold
